title: Question 3.5
statement_text: Is it true that for every tournament $T$, there exists $\prec\in\mathfrak{S}(T)$ such that $\prec$ is both a $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}$-ordering and a $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-ordering?
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. $\mathfrak{S}(T)$ is the set of orderings of $V(T)$; an ordering $\prec$ is an $\overrightarrow{\omega}$-ordering if $\omega(T^{\prec})=\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)$ and a $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-ordering if $\chi(T^{\prec})=\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)$. Using the inequality $\chi(T^{\prec})/\omega(T^{\prec})\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)\le\chi(T^{\prec})$ of Nguyen, Scott and Seymour, valid for every ordering of a tournament, the authors show that every $\overrightarrow{\omega}$-ordering $\prec$ of a tournament $T$ satisfies $\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)\le\chi(T^{\prec})\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)^2$. The question asks whether a single ordering can simultaneously witness both the clique number and the dichromatic number; the authors say they have no reason to believe it, but could not find a counterexample.

title: Question 3.10
statement_text: Is it true that if a class of tournaments $\mathcal{T}$ is polynomially $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-bounded, then so is $\mathcal{T}^{subst}$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. A class (always closed under induced subdigraphs) is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)\le f(\overrightarrow{\omega}(D))$ for every $D$ in the class, polynomially so if $f$ can be taken polynomial. A digraph $D$ is obtained from $D_1$ by substituting $D_2$ for a vertex $u$ of $D_1$ if $D$ is obtained from $D_1-u$ and a disjoint copy of $D_2$ by adding, for each $v\ne u$, all arcs from $V(D_2)$ to $v$ if $uv\in A(D_1)$, all arcs from $v$ to $V(D_2)$ if $vu\in A(D_1)$, and no arc if $u,v$ are non-adjacent; $\mathcal{C}^{subst}$ is the closure of the class $\mathcal{C}$ under substitution. For tournaments $T_1,T_2,T_3$, $\Delta(T_1,T_2,T_3)$ is obtained from disjoint copies of them by adding all arcs from $T_1$ to $T_2$, from $T_2$ to $T_3$ and from $T_3$ to $T_1$ (an integer $k$ stands for $TT_k$, and $\Delta(1,1,1)=\overrightarrow{C_3}$). Define $\widetilde{S}_1=TT_1$ and $\widetilde{S}_n=\Delta(\widetilde{S}_{n-1},\widetilde{S}_{n-1},\widetilde{S}_{n-1})$; then $\overrightarrow{\omega}(\widetilde{S}_n)\ge n$. The authors prove that if a class of tournaments is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded by $f$, then its closure under substitution is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded by $(3wf(w))^w$. The hereditary closure of $\{\widetilde{S}_n\}$ equals $\{TT_1,TT_2,\overrightarrow{C_3}\}^{subst}$, hence satisfies $\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)\le 9^{\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)}$, but it is not known whether this class is polynomially $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded ($\overrightarrow{\chi}(\widetilde{S}_n)$ has order $(3/2)^n$, while the lower bound $n$ on its clique number may be far from tight). The question is motivated by the theorem of Chudnovsky, Penev, Scott and Trotignon that the closure under substitution of a polynomially $\chi$-bounded class of graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded.

title: Conjecture 3.12
statement_text: Let $k\geq 1$. The class of tournaments with twin-width at most $k$ is $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-bounded.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. A class (always closed under induced subdigraphs) is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)\le f(\overrightarrow{\omega}(D))$ for every $D$ in the class, polynomially so if $f$ can be taken polynomial. A contraction sequence of a structure $S$ on $n$ vertices is a sequence of partitions $\mathcal{P}_n,\dots,\mathcal{P}_1$ of $V(S)$ from singletons to a single part, each obtained by merging two parts of the previous one; the error degree of a part $X$ is the number of other parts $Y$ not homogeneous to $X$, and $\operatorname{tww}(S)$ is the minimum over contraction sequences of the maximum error degree. For a tournament, $X$ and $Y$ are not homogeneous if there are arcs in both directions between them; for an ordered tournament $(T,\prec)$ (and similarly an ordered graph), they are also not homogeneous if they interleave, i.e. neither $X\prec Y$ nor $Y\prec X$ holds elementwise. Graphs of bounded twin-width are polynomially $\chi$-bounded (Bourneuf and Thomassé). Define $S_1=TT_1$ and $S_k=\Delta(TT_1,S_{k-1},S_{k-1})$, i.e. a vertex $x$ and two copies $A,B$ of $S_{k-1}$ with all arcs from $x$ to $A$, from $A$ to $B$ and from $B$ to $x$; then $S_k$ has twin-width $1$ and dichromatic number $k$, so tournaments of bounded twin-width can have arbitrarily large dichromatic number. Nevertheless, the authors conjecture that they are $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded, and show that this would follow from the existence, for every tournament, of an ordering $\prec$ with $\omega(T^{\prec})$ bounded in terms of $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)$ and twin-width of the ordered tournament $(T,\prec)$ bounded in terms of that of $T$.

title: Conjecture 3.13
statement_text: There exists a function $f$ such that for every tournament $T$, there exists an ordering $\prec^{*}$ of $V(T)$ such that $\omega(T^{\prec^{*}})\leq f(\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T))$ and $\operatorname{tww}(T,\prec^{*})\leq f(\operatorname{tww}(T))$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. title: Conjecture 3.16
statement_text: There exists a function $f$ such that, for every tournament $T$, there exists a $BST$-ordering $\prec$ of $T$ such that $\omega(T^{\prec})\leq f(\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T))$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. $N^-(x)$ and $N^+(x)$ denote the in- and out-neighbourhood of $x$. Following Geniet and Thomassé, a BST-ordering of a tournament $T$ is (informally) obtained from a rooted binary search tree on $V(T)$ in which, for every vertex $x$, the left child of $x$ and its descendants lie in $N^-(x)$ and the right child of $x$ and its descendants lie in $N^+(x)$; the ordering is the left-to-right order of this tree (recursively: pick $x$, put $N^-(x)$ to its left and $N^+(x)$ to its right, and order both sides in the same way). Geniet and Thomassé proved that the twin-width of the ordered tournament $(T,\prec)$ is bounded by a function of the twin-width of $T$ for every BST-ordering $\prec$. Hence BST-orderings are natural candidates for the authors' conjecture that every tournament has an ordering $\prec$ with $\omega(T^{\prec})$ bounded by a function of $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)$ and twin-width of $(T,\prec)$ bounded by a function of that of $T$, which would imply that tournaments of bounded twin-width are $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded.
notes: The source's grammatical typo 'such:' is normalized to 'such that'.

title: Conjecture 4.3 (Gyárfás-Sumner for Tournaments)
statement_text: A tournament $H$ is $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-binding if and only if $H$ has a backedge graph which is a forest.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. A tournament $H$ is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-binding if the class of tournaments not containing $H$ as a subtournament is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded. This is proposed as the directed analogue of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture (a graph $F$ is $\chi$-binding if and only if it is a forest). The authors prove the 'only if' direction, show it suffices to prove the 'if' direction for trees, and that it is preserved by reversing all arcs and by the composition $H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ (all arcs from $H_1$ to $H_2$). Note however that the final version of the paper remarks that, after submission, the second author (Aubian) disproved this conjecture.

title: Conjecture 4.11
statement_text: Let $(M,\prec)$ be an ordered graph with maximum degree $1$. Then the class of $(M,\prec)$-free ordered graphs is $\chi$-bounded.
context_text: An ordered graph is a pair $(G,\prec)$ where $\prec$ is a total order of $V(G)$; $(H,\prec_H)$ is an induced ordered subgraph of $(G,\prec_G)$ if there is an injection $\phi:V(H)\to V(G)$ preserving both the order and adjacency/non-adjacency, and $(G,\prec_G)$ is $(M,\prec)$-free if it has no induced ordered subgraph isomorphic to $(M,\prec)$. An ordered graph of maximum degree $1$ is an ordered matching (possibly with isolated vertices). A class of ordered graphs is $\chi$-bounded if the class of their underlying graphs is, i.e. $\chi$ is bounded by a function of $\omega$. Briański, Davies and Walczak studied which excluded ordered graphs yield $\chi$-bounded classes and, according to the authors, claimed in a personal communication to have proven that excluding any ordered matching does. The motivation comes from tournaments (orientations of complete graphs): for an ordering $\prec$ of a tournament $T$, the backedge graph $T^{\prec}$ has an edge $uv$ when $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc; with $\overrightarrow{\chi}$ the dichromatic number and $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)=\min_{\prec}\omega(T^{\prec})$, the authors show that the class of $F$-free tournaments has $\overrightarrow{\chi}$ bounded by a function of $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ if and only if the class of ordered graphs excluding all ordered backedge graphs $(F^{\prec},\prec)$ of $F$ is $\chi$-bounded. Hence the conjecture would imply that every tournament with a backedge graph of maximum degree $1$ is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-binding.

title: Conjecture 4.15 (Strong Erdős-Hajnal for Tournaments)
statement_text: A tournament $H$ has the strong Erdős-Hajnal property if and only if it has a backedge graph that is a forest.
context_text: A tournament $H$ has the strong Erdős-Hajnal property if there exists $c$ such that all $H$-free tournaments contain disjoint sets $A$, $B$ with $A\Rightarrow B$ and $|A|,|B|\geq c|H|$. The paper discusses this in connection with Conjecture 4.3, noting that being $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-binding and having the strong Erdős-Hajnal property may coincide.
paper_contribution: The paper discusses the conjecture alongside its own Conjecture 4.3 and notes that no inclusion between $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-binding and the strong Erdős-Hajnal property has been proved, while believing the two conjectures are independent.
notes: Reference [12]: Chudnovsky, Scott, Seymour, Spirkl, European J. Combinatorics 115:103786, 2024.

title: BIG⇒BIG Conjecture
statement_text: The class of all tournaments has the $BIG\Rightarrow BIG$ property.
context_text: A class $\mathcal{T}$ has the $BIG\Rightarrow BIG$ property if there exists $f$ such that, for every $T\in\mathcal{T}$, if $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}(T)\geq f(t)$, then $T$ contains disjoint subtournaments $A$, $B$ with $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}(A),\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}(B)\geq t$ and $A\Rightarrow B$. Nguyen-Scott-Seymour showed it implies the Erdős-El-Zahar conjecture; Klingelhöfer-Newman proved the converse.
paper_contribution: The paper invokes a theorem of Klingelhöfer and Newman (Theorem 4.17) to prove Theorem 4.18 establishing a related structural result about tournaments with the $BIG\Rightarrow BIG$ property.
notes: Reference [22]: Nguyen, Scott, Seymour, 'Some results and problems on tournament structure', 2023.

title: Large dom implies a dom-cluster Conjecture
statement_text: There exist two functions $f$ and $\ell$ such that, for every integer $k$, every tournament $T$ with $\operatorname{dom}(T)\geq f(k)$ contains a subtournament $X$ with $|X|\leq\ell(k)$ and $\operatorname{dom}(X)\geq k$.
context_text: This conjecture of Harutyunyan, Le, Thomassé, and Wu posits that large domination number forces a bounded-size subtournament with large domination number. Since $\operatorname{dom}(T)\leq\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T)\leq\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}(T)$, it is strictly stronger than Theorem 5.1 (large dom implies a $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-cluster).
paper_contribution: The paper introduces Conjecture 5.3 (large dom implies an $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}$-cluster) as an intermediate conjecture between Theorem 5.1 and Conjecture 5.2, and establishes implications among the three statements.
notes: Reference [18]: Harutyunyan, Le, Thomassé, Wu, J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 138, 2017.

title: Conjecture 5.3 (Large dom implies an ω̄-cluster)
statement_text: There exist two functions $f$ and $\ell$ such that, for every integer $k$, every tournament $T$ with $\operatorname{dom}(T)\geq f(k)$ contains a subtournament $X$ with $|X|\leq\ell(k)$ and $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(X)\geq k$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. $N^+(v)$ is the out-neighbourhood of $v$; a dominating set of a tournament $T$ is a set $X$ such that every vertex outside $X$ has an in-neighbour in $X$, and $\operatorname{dom}(T)$ is the minimum size of a dominating set; the authors show $\operatorname{dom}(T)\le\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)$. The authors say that large $\gamma_1$ implies a $\gamma_2$-cluster if there are functions $f,\ell$ such that every tournament $T$ with $\gamma_1(T)\ge f(k)$ has a subtournament $X$ with $|X|\le\ell(k)$ and $\gamma_2(X)\ge k$. title: Rebels = Poset Tournaments Conjecture
statement_text: Every poset tournament is a rebel.
context_text: A tournament $R$ is a rebel if tournaments not containing $R$ have bounded domination number; a poset tournament admits a backedge graph that is a comparability graph. Chudnovsky, Kim, Liu, Seymour and Thomassé proved every rebel is a poset tournament; the converse remains open.
attributed_to: Chudnovsky, Kim, Liu, Seymour and Thomassé
paper_contribution: The paper notes that proving $S_k$ is a rebel for every $k$ would imply Conjecture 5.3, thereby connecting this conjecture to the clique-number framework developed in the paper.
notes: Reference [10]: Chudnovsky, Kim, Liu, Seymour, Thomassé, J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 130:98–113, 2018.

title: Conjecture 5.6
statement_text: There exists a function $g$ such that, for every integer $t$, if $T$ is a tournament such that for every $v\in V(T)$, $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(N^{+}(v))\leq t$, then $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T)\leq g(t)$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. title: Conjecture 5.8 (Large ω̄ implies an ω̄-cluster)
statement_text: There exist two functions $f$ and $\ell$ such that, for every integer $k$, every tournament $T$ with $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T)\geq f(k)$ contains a subtournament $X$ with $|X|\leq\ell(k)$ and $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(X)\geq k$.
context_text: This conjecture strengthens Conjecture 5.3 by replacing the domination-number hypothesis with the clique-number hypothesis. The authors state they believe (or hope) it is true, and note they were not able to disprove even the stronger Question 5.9 where $f$ is the identity function.

title: Question 5.9
statement_text: Is there a function $\ell$ such that, for every tournament $T$, if $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T)\geq k$, then $T$ has a subtournament $A$ such that $|A|\leq\ell(k)$ and $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(A)\geq k$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. The authors conjecture (and 'believe, or maybe only hope') that large clique number implies an $\overrightarrow{\omega}$-cluster: there are functions $f,\ell$ such that every tournament $T$ with $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)\ge f(k)$ contains a subtournament $X$ with $|X|\le\ell(k)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}(X)\ge k$. This question is the stronger form where $f$ is the identity, which they could not answer. Call $T$ $k$-$\overrightarrow{\omega}$-critical if $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)=k$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T-v)=k-1$ for every vertex $v$; the authors observe that their conjecture that there are infinitely many $k$-$\overrightarrow{\omega}$-critical tournaments for every $k\ge3$ would answer this question negatively, and its failure would answer it positively.

title: Conjecture 5.10
statement_text: For every integer $k\geq 3$, there is an infinite number of $k$-$\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}$-critical tournaments.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. A tournament $T$ is $k$-$\overrightarrow{\omega}$-critical if $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)=k$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T-v)=k-1$ for every $v\in V(T)$. The only $1$-$\overrightarrow{\omega}$-critical tournament is the one-vertex tournament and the only $2$-$\overrightarrow{\omega}$-critical one is the directed triangle $\overrightarrow{C_3}$. The authors observe that if the conjecture is true it answers negatively, and if false positively, their question whether there is a function $\ell$ such that every tournament with $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)\ge k$ has a subtournament $A$ with $|A|\le\ell(k)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}(A)\ge k$.

title: Conjecture 6.1
statement_text: If a class of digraphs $\mathcal{C}$ is $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-bounded, then so is its closure under substitution.

For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. A class (always closed under induced subdigraphs) is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)\le f(\overrightarrow{\omega}(D))$ for every $D$ in the class, polynomially so if $f$ can be taken polynomial. A digraph $D$ is obtained from $D_1$ by substituting $D_2$ for a vertex $u$ of $D_1$ if $D$ is obtained from $D_1-u$ and a disjoint copy of $D_2$ by adding, for each $v\ne u$, all arcs from $V(D_2)$ to $v$ if $uv\in A(D_1)$, all arcs from $v$ to $V(D_2)$ if $vu\in A(D_1)$, and no arc if $u,v$ are non-adjacent; $\mathcal{C}^{subst}$ is the closure of the class $\mathcal{C}$ under substitution. The authors prove that the closure under substitution of a $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded class of tournaments is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded (by $(3wf(w))^w$ if the class is bounded by $f$), and that the same holds for a class of digraphs whose underlying graphs have chromatic number at most $K$ (with bound $(3K)^w$). The general digraph case is harder because the inequality $\chi(D^{\prec})/\omega(D^{\prec})\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$, valid for every ordering of a tournament and used for most of the tournament results, fails for digraphs (orient a triangle-free graph of large chromatic number acyclically); it extends only to digraphs of bounded independence number. The authors nevertheless believe that the substitution result generalises to all digraphs.
